            break
    return r


def hankel_rank(f: Series, alphabet: str, depth: int) -> int:
    """Rank of the truncated Hankel matrix [ f(uv) ]_{|u|,|v| <= depth}.  By the
    Kleene-Schuetzenberger theorem, f is representative exactly when these ranks
    stay bounded as depth grows, and the limiting rank is the minimal dimension
    of a linear representation of f."""
    rows = all_words(alphabet, depth)
    cols = all_words(alphabet, depth)
    return rank([[f(u + v) for v in cols] for u in rows])


def determinant(matrix: List[List[Fraction]]) -> Fraction:
    """Exact determinant by fraction-free-style Gaussian elimination."""
    m = [row[:] for row in matrix]
    n = len(m)
    det = Fraction(1)
    for c in range(n):
        piv = next((i for i in range(c, n) if m[i][c] != 0), None)
        if piv is None:
            return Fraction(0)
        if piv != c:
            m[c], m[piv] = m[piv], m[c]
            det = -det
        det *= m[c][c]
        inv = m[c][c]
        m[c] = [x / inv for x in m[c]]
        for i in range(c + 1, n):
            if m[i][c] != 0:
                factor = m[i][c]
                m[i] = [x - factor * y for x, y in zip(m[i], m[c])]
    return det


def matrix_mul(a: List[List[Fraction]], b: List[List[Fraction]]) -> List[List[Fraction]]:
    n, k, p = len(a), len(b), len(b[0])
    return [[sum((a[i][t] * b[t][j] for t in range(k)), Fraction(0)) for j in range(p)]
            for i in range(n)]


def word_matrix(mu: Dict[str, List[List[Fraction]]], word: Word, dim: int) -> List[List[Fraction]]:
    """The multiplicative extension mu : X* -> M_n(K) of a map on letters."""
    out = [[Fraction(1) if i == j else Fraction(0) for j in range(dim)] for i in range(dim)]
    for a in word:
        out = matrix_mul(out, mu[a])
    return out


def linear_rep_series(lam: List[Fraction], mu: Dict[str, List[List[Fraction]]],
                      gam: List[Fraction]) -> Series:
    """The series w |-> lambda mu(w) gamma attached to a linear representation."""
    dim = len(lam)

    def f(word: Word) -> Fraction:
        m = word_matrix(mu, word, dim)
        return sum((lam[i] * m[i][j] * gam[j] for i in range(dim) for j in range(dim)),
                   Fraction(0))
    return f


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstrations
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demo_shuffle_basics() -> None:
    print("=" * 76)
    print("1. The shuffle product of words")
    print("=" * 76)
    u, v = w("ab"), w("c")
    print(f"  {show(u)} shuffle {show(v)} = "
          + " + ".join(f"{m}·{show(z)}" for z, m in sorted(shuffle(u, v).items())))
    u, v = w("a"), w("a")
    print(f"  {show(u)} shuffle {show(v)} = "
          + " + ".join(f"{m}·{show(z)}" for z, m in sorted(shuffle(u, v).items()))
          + "     (multiplicity 2: the shuffle is a *multiset*)")

    print("\n  Cardinality |u shuffle v| = C(|u|+|v|, |u|):")
    ok = True
    for u in all_words("ab", 3):
        for v in all_words("ab", 3):
            card = sum(shuffle(u, v).values())
            expected = comb(len(u) + len(v), len(u))
            ok &= (card == expected)
    print(f"    verified for all |u|,|v| <= 3 over {{a,b}}: {ok}")

    print("\n  Commutativity and associativity:")
    words = all_words("ab", 2)
    comm = all(shuffle(u, v) == shuffle(v, u) for u in words for v in words)

    def shuffle3_left(u: Word, x: Word, y: Word) -> Counter:
        out: Counter = Counter()
        for z, m in shuffle(u, x).items():
            for t, n in shuffle(z, y).items():
                out[t] += m * n
        return out

    def shuffle3_right(u: Word, x: Word, y: Word) -> Counter:
        out: Counter = Counter()
        for z, m in shuffle(x, y).items():
            for t, n in shuffle(u, z).items():
                out[t] += m * n
        return out

    assoc = all(shuffle3_left(a, b, c) == shuffle3_right(a, b, c)
                for a in words for b in words for c in words)
    print(f"    u shuffle v = v shuffle u                : {comm}")
    print(f"    (u shuffle v) shuffle t = u shuffle (v shuffle t) : {assoc}")


def demo_duality() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 76)
    print("2. Shuffle/unshuffle duality and the two bialgebra axioms")
    print("=" * 76)
    word = w("aba")
    print(f"  Delta_sh({show(word)}) = "
          + " + ".join(f"{m}·({show(p)} ⊗ {show(q)})"
                       for (p, q), m in sorted(unshuffle(word).items())))
    print(f"  it has 2^{len(word)} = {sum(unshuffle(word).values())} terms.")

    words = all_words("ab", 3)
    dual = True
    for u in all_words("ab", 2):
        for v in all_words("ab", 2):
            sh = shuffle(u, v)
            for z in words:
                if sh[z] != unshuffle(z)[(u, v)]:
                    dual = False
    print(f"\n  Duality  <u shuffle v, z> = <u ⊗ v, Delta_sh(z)>  : {dual}")

    bialg = all(unshuffle(u + v) == pair_mul(unshuffle(u), unshuffle(v))
                for u in all_words("ab", 2) for v in all_words("ab", 2))
    print(f"  Bialgebra axiom  Delta_sh(uv) = Delta_sh(u)·Delta_sh(v) : {bialg}")

    cocomm = all(Counter({(q, p): m for (p, q), m in unshuffle(z).items()}) == unshuffle(z)
                 for z in words)
    print(f"  Cocommutativity of Delta_sh                             : {cocomm}")

    def co_left(z: Word) -> Counter:
        out: Counter = Counter()
        for (p, q), m in unshuffle(z).items():
            for (p1, p2), n in unshuffle(p).items():
                out[(p1, p2, q)] += m * n
        return out

    def co_right(z: Word) -> Counter:
        out: Counter = Counter()
        for (p, q), m in unshuffle(z).items():
            for (q1, q2), n in unshuffle(q).items():
                out[(p, q1, q2)] += m * n
        return out

    coassoc = all(co_left(z) == co_right(z) for z in words)
    print(f"  Coassociativity of Delta_sh                             : {coassoc}")

    print("\n  The dual bialgebra (shuffle, deconcatenation):")
    word = w("abc")
    print(f"    Delta_dec({show(word)}) = "
          + " + ".join(f"({show(p)} ⊗ {show(q)})"
                       for (p, q), _ in sorted(deconcat(word).items())))
    axiom = all(bind_deconcat(shuffle(u, v)) == deconc_shuffle_prod(u, v)
                for u in all_words("ab", 2) for v in all_words("ab", 2))
    print("    Bialgebra axiom  Delta_dec(u shuffle v) = "
          f"Delta_dec(u) shuffle_2 Delta_dec(v) : {axiom}")


def demo_characters() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 76)
    print("3. Characters: Kleene stars of planes vs. exponentials of planes")
    print("=" * 76)
    c = {"a": Fraction(2), "b": Fraction(-3)}
    words = all_words("ab", 3)
    ps, ep = plane_star(c), exp_plane(c)
    print(f"  plane l = 2a - 3b")
    print(f"    l*   : (l*|ab)   = {ps(w('ab'))},  (l*|aab) = {ps(w('aab'))}")
    print(f"    e^l  : (e^l|ab)  = {ep(w('ab'))},  (e^l|aab) = {ep(w('aab'))}")
    print(f"    l* is a concatenation character : {is_concat_character(ps, words)}")
    print(f"    e^l is a shuffle character      : {is_shuffle_character(ep, all_words('ab', 2))}")
    print(f"    l* is a shuffle character       : "
          f"{is_shuffle_character(ps, all_words('ab', 2))}   (only if l = 0)")

    print("\n  Divided powers: any shuffle character satisfies f(a^n) = f(a)^n / n!")
    for n in range(6):
        lhs = ep((("a",) * n))
        rhs = ep(w("a")) ** n / factorial(n)
        print(f"    n = {n}:  f(a^{n}) = {lhs}   f(a)^{n}/{n}! = {rhs}   equal: {lhs == rhs}")

    print("\n  Infinitesimal characters of the concatenation bialgebra are the planes:")
    g = {(): Fraction(0), ("a",): Fraction(5), ("b",): Fraction(7)}

    def plane(word: Word) -> Fraction:
        return g.get(word, Fraction(0))

    ok = all(plane(u + v) == plane(u) * counit(v) + counit(u) * plane(v)
             for u in words for v in words)
    print(f"    g = 5a + 7b is a derivation for concatenation: {ok}")

    def not_plane(word: Word) -> Fraction:
        return Fraction(1) if word == w("ab") else Fraction(0)

    bad = [(u, v) for u in words for v in words
           if not_plane(u + v) != not_plane(u) * counit(v) + counit(u) * not_plane(v)]
    print(f"    g = ab (length 2) fails, first witness (u,v) = "
          f"({show(bad[0][0])}, {show(bad[0][1])})")


def demo_representative() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 76)
    print("4. Representative functions and the Kleene-Schuetzenberger theorem")
    print("=" * 76)
    # f(w) = number of occurrences of the letter 'a': a rank-2 rational series.
    lam = [Fraction(1), Fraction(0)]
    gam = [Fraction(0), Fraction(1)]
    mu = {
        "a": [[Fraction(1), Fraction(1)], [Fraction(0), Fraction(1)]],
        "b": [[Fraction(1), Fraction(0)], [Fraction(0), Fraction(1)]],
    }
    count_a = linear_rep_series(lam, mu, gam)
    print("  f(w) = |w|_a (number of a's) has the 2-dimensional representation")
    print("     lambda = (1,0),  mu(a) = [[1,1],[0,1]],  mu(b) = I,  gamma = (0,1)")
    for word in [w(""), w("a"), w("ab"), w("aab"), w("baba")]:
        print(f"     f({show(word):>5}) = {count_a(word)}")
    print(f"  Hankel ranks at depths 1,2,3 : "
          f"{[hankel_rank(count_a, 'ab', d) for d in (1, 2, 3)]}   (stabilises at 2)")

    print("\n  Factorisation f(uv) = sum_i g_i(u) h_i(v) read off the representation:")
    ok = True
    for u in all_words("ab", 3):
        for v in all_words("ab", 3):
            g1, g2 = count_a(u), Fraction(1)
            h1, h2 = Fraction(1), count_a(v)
            ok &= (count_a(u + v) == g1 * h1 + g2 * h2)
    print(f"     |uv|_a = |u|_a·1 + 1·|v|_a for all |u|,|v| <= 3 : {ok}")

    print("\n  Rationality is preserved by the shuffle product of series:")
    two_pow = linear_rep_series([Fraction(1)], {"a": [[Fraction(2)]], "b": [[Fraction(2)]]},
                                [Fraction(1)])
    prod = shuffle_series(count_a, two_pow)
    print(f"     f = |w|_a  (rank 2),  g = 2^|w|  (rank 1)")
    for word in [w(""), w("a"), w("ab"), w("aba")]:
        print(f"     (f shuffle g)({show(word):>4}) = {prod(word)}")
    print(f"     Hankel ranks of f shuffle g at depths 1,2,3 : "
          f"{[hankel_rank(prod, 'ab', d) for d in (1, 2, 3)]}   (bounded: still rational)")

    print("\n  The shuffle of series extends the shuffle of words:")
    u, v = w("ab"), w("a")

    def dirac(x: Word) -> Series:
        return lambda z: Fraction(1) if z == x else Fraction(0)

    dprod = shuffle_series(dirac(u), dirac(v))
    sh = shuffle(u, v)
    ok = all(dprod(z) == sh[z] for z in all_words("ab", 3))
    print(f"     (delta_{show(u)} shuffle delta_{show(v)})(z) = multiplicity of z "
          f"in {show(u)} shuffle {show(v)} : {ok}")

    print("\n  The counit is the unit, and the shuffle of series is associative:")
    words = all_words("ab", 3)
    unit_ok = all(shuffle_series(counit, count_a)(z) == count_a(z) for z in words)
    left = shuffle_series(shuffle_series(count_a, two_pow), counit)
    right = shuffle_series(count_a, shuffle_series(two_pow, counit))
    assoc_ok = all(left(z) == right(z) for z in words)
    print(f"     eps shuffle f = f : {unit_ok}     associativity : {assoc_ok}")


def demo_separation() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 76)
    print("5. The separation theorem: group-like series are never rational")
    print("=" * 76)
    print("  The Hankel matrix of exp(a) restricted to the powers of a is [1/(i+j)!].")
    print("  Its leading minors are nonzero, so its rank is infinite:")
    for n in range(1, 8):
        m = [[Fraction(1, factorial(i + j)) for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]
        d = determinant(m)
        print(f"    n = {n}: det [1/(i+j)!]_{{0<=i,j<{n}}} = {d}  (nonzero: {d != 0})")

    c = {"a": Fraction(1)}
    ep = exp_plane(c)
    print("\n  Hankel ranks of exp(a) at growing depths (over the one-letter alphabet):")
    print(f"    {[hankel_rank(ep, 'a', d) for d in (1, 2, 3, 4, 5)]}   -> unbounded")
    print("  Hence exp(l) is a shuffle character which is NOT representative,")
    print("  while the Kleene star l* is representative of rank one but is a shuffle")
    print("  character only in the degenerate case l = 0: the two character groups of")
    print("  the two bialgebras meet exactly in the counit.")


def main() -> None:
    demo_shuffle_basics()
    demo_duality()
    demo_characters()
    demo_representative()
    demo_separation()
    print()
    print("All demonstrations completed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

demos.name: Complete Numerical Tour of the Two Bialgebras and the Rationality Divide
demos.description: An exact-arithmetic tour of every result in the paper. It enumerates shuffle products with multiplicities and checks the binomial cardinality, commutativity and associativity; prints the unshuffle and deconcatenation coproducts of a word and verifies shuffle/unshuffle duality, cocommutativity, coassociativity and both bialgebra axioms; contrasts the Kleene star of a plane (a concatenation character) with the exponential of a plane (a shuffle character) and checks the divided-power identity f(a^n) = f(a)^n / n!; builds an explicit two-dimensional linear representation of the letter-counting series and confirms its Hankel ranks stabilise; shows that the shuffle product of two rational series is again rational; and finally exhibits the separation, computing the nonzero leading minors of the factorial Hankel matrix [1/(i+j)!] and the unbounded Hankel ranks of the exponential series. All computations use fractions of arbitrary-precision integers, so no conclusion depends on floating-point tolerance.
demos.code:
"""
Various Bialgebras of Representative Functions on Free Monoids
==============================================================

Self-contained numerical demonstrations of the results of the accompanying
paper.  Everything is computed exactly (integers and rationals); no external
libraries beyond the Python standard library are used.

The objects.  Let X be a finite alphabet and X* the free monoid of words.
On the vector space K<X> spanned by words we study two dual bialgebra
structures:

    (K<X>, concatenation, Delta_shuffle)   graded, noncommutative, cocommutative
    (K<X>, shuffle,       Delta_deconcat)  graded, commutative,   co-noncommutative

and the "series" side K<<X>> = functions f : X* -> K, where the pairing
<f, w> = f(w) makes shuffle and unshuffle adjoint.

The demonstrations below verify, on explicit data:

  1. the shuffle product of words: commutativity, associativity, and the
     binomial cardinality |u shuffle v| = C(|u|+|v|, |u|);
  2. shuffle/unshuffle duality: <u shuffle v, w> = <u tensor v, Delta_sh(w)>;
  3. the bialgebra axiom Delta_sh(uv) = Delta_sh(u) Delta_sh(v), plus
     coassociativity and cocommutativity of Delta_sh;
  4. the bialgebra axiom Delta_dec(u shuffle v) = Delta_dec(u) shuffle_2
     Delta_dec(v) for the deconcatenation coproduct;
  5. characters: Kleene stars of planes are exactly the concatenation
     characters; exponentials of planes are shuffle characters, with the
     divided-power values f(a^n) = f(a)^n / n!;
  6. Kleene-Schuetzenberger: a function is representative iff it has a finite
     dimensional space of left translates iff it has a linear representation;
  7. rationality is stable under the shuffle product of series;
  8. the separation theorem: exp(l) is a shuffle character of infinite Hankel
     rank, hence not representative, while the Kleene star l* is representative
     of rank one but is not a shuffle character unless l = 0.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from collections import Counter
from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import product
from math import comb, factorial
from typing import Callable, Dict, Iterable, List, Tuple

Word = Tuple[str, ...]
Pair = Tuple[Word, Word]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Words, shuffle product, coproducts
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def w(s: str) -> Word:
    """Turn the string 's' into a word (a tuple of one-letter symbols)."""
    return tuple(s)


def show(word: Word) -> str:
    """Render a word; the empty word is printed as '1'."""
    return "".join(word) if word else "1"


def shuffle(u: Word, v: Word) -> Counter:
    """The multiset u shuffle v of all interleavings of u and v, with
    multiplicity, computed by the classical recursion

        1 shuffle v = v,  u shuffle 1 = u,
        au shuffle bv = a (u shuffle bv) + b (au shuffle v).

    The result has C(|u|+|v|, |u|) elements counted with multiplicity."""
    if not u:
        return Counter({v: 1})
    if not v:
        return Counter({u: 1})
    out: Counter = Counter()
    for z, m in shuffle(u[1:], v).items():
        out[(u[0],) + z] += m
    for z, m in shuffle(u, v[1:]).items():
        out[(v[0],) + z] += m
    return out


def unshuffle(word: Word) -> Counter:
    """The unshuffle coproduct Delta_sh(w) = sum over splittings of the
    positions of w into two complementary subsequences, given by the recursion
    Delta_sh(aw) = (a tensor 1 + 1 tensor a) . Delta_sh(w).  It has exactly
    2^|w| terms with multiplicity."""
    if not word:
        return Counter({((), ()): 1})
    a, rest = word[0], word[1:]
    out: Counter = Counter()
    for (p, q), m in unshuffle(rest).items():
        out[((a,) + p, q)] += m
        out[(p, (a,) + q)] += m
    return out


def deconcat(word: Word) -> Counter:
    """The deconcatenation coproduct Delta_dec(w) = sum_{w = z1 z2} z1 tensor z2.
    It has exactly |w| + 1 terms, each with multiplicity one."""
    return Counter({(word[:k], word[k:]): 1 for k in range(len(word) + 1)})


def pair_mul(s: Counter, t: Counter) -> Counter:
    """Componentwise concatenation of tensors: the product of the tensor square
    for the concatenation product."""
    out: Counter = Counter()
    for (p1, p2), m in s.items():
        for (q1, q2), n in t.items():
            out[(p1 + q1, p2 + q2)] += m * n
    return out


def shuffle_pair(p: Pair, q: Pair) -> Counter:
    """Shuffle product of two elementary tensors: (p1 tensor p2) shuffle_2
    (q1 tensor q2) = (p1 shuffle q1) tensor (p2 shuffle q2)."""
    out: Counter = Counter()
    for r, m in shuffle(p[0], q[0]).items():
        for s, n in shuffle(p[1], q[1]).items():
            out[(r, s)] += m * n
    return out


def bind_deconcat(s: Counter) -> Counter:
    """Apply Delta_dec linearly to a multiset of words."""
    out: Counter = Counter()
    for z, m in s.items():
        for pr, n in deconcat(z).items():
            out[pr] += m * n
    return out


def deconc_shuffle_prod(u: Word, v: Word) -> Counter:
    """Delta_dec(u) shuffle_2 Delta_dec(v)."""
    out: Counter = Counter()
    for p, m in deconcat(u).items():
        for q, n in deconcat(v).items():
            for pr, k in shuffle_pair(p, q).items():
                out[pr] += m * n * k
    return out


def all_words(alphabet: str, max_len: int) -> List[Word]:
    """All words over 'alphabet' of length at most 'max_len', in shortlex order."""
    out: List[Word] = []
    for n in range(max_len + 1):
        out.extend(product(tuple(alphabet), repeat=n))
    return out


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Series, shuffle of series, characters
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

Series = Callable[[Word], Fraction]


def shuffle_series(f: Series, g: Series) -> Series:
    """The shuffle product of two series, defined coefficientwise through the
    unshuffle coproduct:  (f shuffle g)(w) = sum_{(u,v) in Delta_sh(w)} f(u)g(v)."""
    def h(word: Word) -> Fraction:
        return sum((Fraction(m) * f(p) * g(q) for (p, q), m in unshuffle(word).items()),
                   Fraction(0))
    return h


def counit(word: Word) -> Fraction:
    """The counit: 1 on the empty word, 0 elsewhere; unit for the shuffle
    product of series."""
    return Fraction(1) if not word else Fraction(0)


def plane_star(c: Dict[str, Fraction]) -> Series:
    """The Kleene star l* of the plane l = sum_x c_x x: the monoid morphism
    w = x1...xn  |->  c_{x1} ... c_{xn}.  These are exactly the characters of
    the concatenation bialgebra."""
    def f(word: Word) -> Fraction:
        out = Fraction(1)
        for a in word:
            out *= c[a]
        return out
    return f


def exp_plane(c: Dict[str, Fraction]) -> Series:
    """The exponential exp(l) of the plane l = sum_x c_x x: the series whose
    coefficient at a word of length n is c_{x1}...c_{xn} / n!.  These are
    characters of the shuffle algebra (group-like for Delta_sh)."""
    def f(word: Word) -> Fraction:
        out = Fraction(1)
        for a in word:
            out *= c[a]
        return out / factorial(len(word))
    return f


def is_concat_character(f: Series, words: Iterable[Word]) -> bool:
    """Test f(1) = 1 and f(uv) = f(u) f(v) on the supplied words."""
    if f(()) != 1:
        return False
    return all(f(u + v) == f(u) * f(v) for u in words for v in words)


def is_shuffle_character(f: Series, words: Iterable[Word]) -> bool:
    """Test f(1) = 1 and f(u) f(v) = sum_{z in u shuffle v} f(z)."""
    if f(()) != 1:
        return False
    for u in words:
        for v in words:
            rhs = sum((Fraction(m) * f(z) for z, m in shuffle(u, v).items()), Fraction(0))
            if f(u) * f(v) != rhs:
                return False
    return True


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Representative functions: Hankel rank and linear representations
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def rank(matrix: List[List[Fraction]]) -> int:
    """Exact rank of a rational matrix by Gaussian elimination."""
    m = [row[:] for row in matrix]
    rows, cols = len(m), (len(m[0]) if m else 0)
    r = 0
    for c in range(cols):
        piv = next((i for i in range(r, rows) if m[i][c] != 0), None)
        if piv is None:
            continue
        m[r], m[piv] = m[piv], m[r]
        pivot = m[r][c]
        m[r] = [x / pivot for x in m[r]]
        for i in range(rows):
            if i != r and m[i][c] != 0:
                factor = m[i][c]
                m[i] = [x - factor * y for x, y in zip(m[i], m[r])]
        r += 1
        if r == rows:
            break
    return r


def hankel_rank(f: Series, alphabet: str, depth: int) -> int:
    """Rank of the truncated Hankel matrix [ f(uv) ]_{|u|,|v| <= depth}.  By the
    Kleene-Schuetzenberger theorem, f is representative exactly when these ranks
    stay bounded as depth grows, and the limiting rank is the minimal dimension
    of a linear representation of f."""
    rows = all_words(alphabet, depth)
    cols = all_words(alphabet, depth)
    return rank([[f(u + v) for v in cols] for u in rows])


def determinant(matrix: List[List[Fraction]]) -> Fraction:
    """Exact determinant by fraction-free-style Gaussian elimination."""
    m = [row[:] for row in matrix]
    n = len(m)
    det = Fraction(1)
    for c in range(n):
        piv = next((i for i in range(c, n) if m[i][c] != 0), None)
        if piv is None:
            return Fraction(0)
        if piv != c:
            m[c], m[piv] = m[piv], m[c]
            det = -det
        det *= m[c][c]
        inv = m[c][c]
        m[c] = [x / inv for x in m[c]]
        for i in range(c + 1, n):
            if m[i][c] != 0:
                factor = m[i][c]
                m[i] = [x - factor * y for x, y in zip(m[i], m[c])]
    return det


def matrix_mul(a: List[List[Fraction]], b: List[List[Fraction]]) -> List[List[Fraction]]:
    n, k, p = len(a), len(b), len(b[0])
    return [[sum((a[i][t] * b[t][j] for t in range(k)), Fraction(0)) for j in range(p)]
            for i in range(n)]


def word_matrix(mu: Dict[str, List[List[Fraction]]], word: Word, dim: int) -> List[List[Fraction]]:
    """The multiplicative extension mu : X* -> M_n(K) of a map on letters."""
    out = [[Fraction(1) if i == j else Fraction(0) for j in range(dim)] for i in range(dim)]
    for a in word:
        out = matrix_mul(out, mu[a])
    return out


def linear_rep_series(lam: List[Fraction], mu: Dict[str, List[List[Fraction]]],
                      gam: List[Fraction]) -> Series:
    """The series w |-> lambda mu(w) gamma attached to a linear representation."""
    dim = len(lam)

    def f(word: Word) -> Fraction:
        m = word_matrix(mu, word, dim)
        return sum((lam[i] * m[i][j] * gam[j] for i in range(dim) for j in range(dim)),
                   Fraction(0))
    return f


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstrations
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demo_shuffle_basics() -> None:
    print("=" * 76)
    print("1. The shuffle product of words")
    print("=" * 76)
    u, v = w("ab"), w("c")
    print(f"  {show(u)} shuffle {show(v)} = "
          + " + ".join(f"{m}·{show(z)}" for z, m in sorted(shuffle(u, v).items())))
    u, v = w("a"), w("a")
    print(f"  {show(u)} shuffle {show(v)} = "
          + " + ".join(f"{m}·{show(z)}" for z, m in sorted(shuffle(u, v).items()))
          + "     (multiplicity 2: the shuffle is a *multiset*)")

    print("\n  Cardinality |u shuffle v| = C(|u|+|v|, |u|):")
    ok = True
    for u in all_words("ab", 3):
        for v in all_words("ab", 3):
            card = sum(shuffle(u, v).values())
            expected = comb(len(u) + len(v), len(u))
            ok &= (card == expected)
    print(f"    verified for all |u|,|v| <= 3 over {{a,b}}: {ok}")

    print("\n  Commutativity and associativity:")
    words = all_words("ab", 2)
    comm = all(shuffle(u, v) == shuffle(v, u) for u in words for v in words)

    def shuffle3_left(u: Word, x: Word, y: Word) -> Counter:
        out: Counter = Counter()
        for z, m in shuffle(u, x).items():
            for t, n in shuffle(z, y).items():
                out[t] += m * n
        return out

    def shuffle3_right(u: Word, x: Word, y: Word) -> Counter:
        out: Counter = Counter()
        for z, m in shuffle(x, y).items():
            for t, n in shuffle(u, z).items():
                out[t] += m * n
        return out

    assoc = all(shuffle3_left(a, b, c) == shuffle3_right(a, b, c)
                for a in words for b in words for c in words)
    print(f"    u shuffle v = v shuffle u                : {comm}")
    print(f"    (u shuffle v) shuffle t = u shuffle (v shuffle t) : {assoc}")


def demo_duality() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 76)
    print("2. Shuffle/unshuffle duality and the two bialgebra axioms")
    print("=" * 76)
    word = w("aba")
    print(f"  Delta_sh({show(word)}) = "
          + " + ".join(f"{m}·({show(p)} ⊗ {show(q)})"
                       for (p, q), m in sorted(unshuffle(word).items())))
    print(f"  it has 2^{len(word)} = {sum(unshuffle(word).values())} terms.")

    words = all_words("ab", 3)
    dual = True
    for u in all_words("ab", 2):
        for v in all_words("ab", 2):
            sh = shuffle(u, v)
            for z in words:
                if sh[z] != unshuffle(z)[(u, v)]:
                    dual = False
    print(f"\n  Duality  <u shuffle v, z> = <u ⊗ v, Delta_sh(z)>  : {dual}")

    bialg = all(unshuffle(u + v) == pair_mul(unshuffle(u), unshuffle(v))
                for u in all_words("ab", 2) for v in all_words("ab", 2))
    print(f"  Bialgebra axiom  Delta_sh(uv) = Delta_sh(u)·Delta_sh(v) : {bialg}")

    cocomm = all(Counter({(q, p): m for (p, q), m in unshuffle(z).items()}) == unshuffle(z)
                 for z in words)
    print(f"  Cocommutativity of Delta_sh                             : {cocomm}")

    def co_left(z: Word) -> Counter:
        out: Counter = Counter()
        for (p, q), m in unshuffle(z).items():
            for (p1, p2), n in unshuffle(p).items():
                out[(p1, p2, q)] += m * n
        return out

    def co_right(z: Word) -> Counter:
        out: Counter = Counter()
        for (p, q), m in unshuffle(z).items():
            for (q1, q2), n in unshuffle(q).items():
                out[(p, q1, q2)] += m * n
        return out

    coassoc = all(co_left(z) == co_right(z) for z in words)
    print(f"  Coassociativity of Delta_sh                             : {coassoc}")

    print("\n  The dual bialgebra (shuffle, deconcatenation):")
    word = w("abc")
    print(f"    Delta_dec({show(word)}) = "
          + " + ".join(f"({show(p)} ⊗ {show(q)})"
                       for (p, q), _ in sorted(deconcat(word).items())))
    axiom = all(bind_deconcat(shuffle(u, v)) == deconc_shuffle_prod(u, v)
                for u in all_words("ab", 2) for v in all_words("ab", 2))
    print("    Bialgebra axiom  Delta_dec(u shuffle v) = "
          f"Delta_dec(u) shuffle_2 Delta_dec(v) : {axiom}")


def demo_characters() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 76)
    print("3. Characters: Kleene stars of planes vs. exponentials of planes")
    print("=" * 76)
    c = {"a": Fraction(2), "b": Fraction(-3)}
    words = all_words("ab", 3)
    ps, ep = plane_star(c), exp_plane(c)
    print(f"  plane l = 2a - 3b")
    print(f"    l*   : (l*|ab)   = {ps(w('ab'))},  (l*|aab) = {ps(w('aab'))}")
    print(f"    e^l  : (e^l|ab)  = {ep(w('ab'))},  (e^l|aab) = {ep(w('aab'))}")
    print(f"    l* is a concatenation character : {is_concat_character(ps, words)}")
    print(f"    e^l is a shuffle character      : {is_shuffle_character(ep, all_words('ab', 2))}")
    print(f"    l* is a shuffle character       : "
          f"{is_shuffle_character(ps, all_words('ab', 2))}   (only if l = 0)")

    print("\n  Divided powers: any shuffle character satisfies f(a^n) = f(a)^n / n!")
    for n in range(6):
        lhs = ep((("a",) * n))
        rhs = ep(w("a")) ** n / factorial(n)
        print(f"    n = {n}:  f(a^{n}) = {lhs}   f(a)^{n}/{n}! = {rhs}   equal: {lhs == rhs}")

    print("\n  Infinitesimal characters of the concatenation bialgebra are the planes:")
    g = {(): Fraction(0), ("a",): Fraction(5), ("b",): Fraction(7)}

    def plane(word: Word) -> Fraction:
        return g.get(word, Fraction(0))

    ok = all(plane(u + v) == plane(u) * counit(v) + counit(u) * plane(v)
             for u in words for v in words)
    print(f"    g = 5a + 7b is a derivation for concatenation: {ok}")

    def not_plane(word: Word) -> Fraction:
        return Fraction(1) if word == w("ab") else Fraction(0)

    bad = [(u, v) for u in words for v in words
           if not_plane(u + v) != not_plane(u) * counit(v) + counit(u) * not_plane(v)]
    print(f"    g = ab (length 2) fails, first witness (u,v) = "
          f"({show(bad[0][0])}, {show(bad[0][1])})")


def demo_representative() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 76)
    print("4. Representative functions and the Kleene-Schuetzenberger theorem")
    print("=" * 76)
    # f(w) = number of occurrences of the letter 'a': a rank-2 rational series.
    lam = [Fraction(1), Fraction(0)]
    gam = [Fraction(0), Fraction(1)]
    mu = {
        "a": [[Fraction(1), Fraction(1)], [Fraction(0), Fraction(1)]],
        "b": [[Fraction(1), Fraction(0)], [Fraction(0), Fraction(1)]],
    }
    count_a = linear_rep_series(lam, mu, gam)
    print("  f(w) = |w|_a (number of a's) has the 2-dimensional representation")
    print("     lambda = (1,0),  mu(a) = [[1,1],[0,1]],  mu(b) = I,  gamma = (0,1)")
    for word in [w(""), w("a"), w("ab"), w("aab"), w("baba")]:
        print(f"     f({show(word):>5}) = {count_a(word)}")
    print(f"  Hankel ranks at depths 1,2,3 : "
          f"{[hankel_rank(count_a, 'ab', d) for d in (1, 2, 3)]}   (stabilises at 2)")

    print("\n  Factorisation f(uv) = sum_i g_i(u) h_i(v) read off the representation:")
    ok = True
    for u in all_words("ab", 3):
        for v in all_words("ab", 3):
            g1, g2 = count_a(u), Fraction(1)
            h1, h2 = Fraction(1), count_a(v)
            ok &= (count_a(u + v) == g1 * h1 + g2 * h2)
    print(f"     |uv|_a = |u|_a·1 + 1·|v|_a for all |u|,|v| <= 3 : {ok}")

    print("\n  Rationality is preserved by the shuffle product of series:")
    two_pow = linear_rep_series([Fraction(1)], {"a": [[Fraction(2)]], "b": [[Fraction(2)]]},
                                [Fraction(1)])
    prod = shuffle_series(count_a, two_pow)
    print(f"     f = |w|_a  (rank 2),  g = 2^|w|  (rank 1)")
    for word in [w(""), w("a"), w("ab"), w("aba")]:
        print(f"     (f shuffle g)({show(word):>4}) = {prod(word)}")
    print(f"     Hankel ranks of f shuffle g at depths 1,2,3 : "
          f"{[hankel_rank(prod, 'ab', d) for d in (1, 2, 3)]}   (bounded: still rational)")

    print("\n  The shuffle of series extends the shuffle of words:")
    u, v = w("ab"), w("a")

    def dirac(x: Word) -> Series:
        return lambda z: Fraction(1) if z == x else Fraction(0)

    dprod = shuffle_series(dirac(u), dirac(v))
    sh = shuffle(u, v)
    ok = all(dprod(z) == sh[z] for z in all_words("ab", 3))
    print(f"     (delta_{show(u)} shuffle delta_{show(v)})(z) = multiplicity of z "
          f"in {show(u)} shuffle {show(v)} : {ok}")

    print("\n  The counit is the unit, and the shuffle of series is associative:")
    words = all_words("ab", 3)
    unit_ok = all(shuffle_series(counit, count_a)(z) == count_a(z) for z in words)
    left = shuffle_series(shuffle_series(count_a, two_pow), counit)
    right = shuffle_series(count_a, shuffle_series(two_pow, counit))
    assoc_ok = all(left(z) == right(z) for z in words)
    print(f"     eps shuffle f = f : {unit_ok}     associativity : {assoc_ok}")


def demo_separation() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 76)
    print("5. The separation theorem: group-like series are never rational")
    print("=" * 76)
    print("  The Hankel matrix of exp(a) restricted to the powers of a is [1/(i+j)!].")
    print("  Its leading minors are nonzero, so its rank is infinite:")
    for n in range(1, 8):
        m = [[Fraction(1, factorial(i + j)) for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]
        d = determinant(m)
        print(f"    n = {n}: det [1/(i+j)!]_{{0<=i,j<{n}}} = {d}  (nonzero: {d != 0})")

    c = {"a": Fraction(1)}
    ep = exp_plane(c)
    print("\n  Hankel ranks of exp(a) at growing depths (over the one-letter alphabet):")
    print(f"    {[hankel_rank(ep, 'a', d) for d in (1, 2, 3, 4, 5)]}   -> unbounded")
    print("  Hence exp(l) is a shuffle character which is NOT representative,")
    print("  while the Kleene star l* is representative of rank one but is a shuffle")
    print("  character only in the degenerate case l = 0: the two character groups of")
    print("  the two bialgebras meet exactly in the counit.")


def main() -> None:
    demo_shuffle_basics()
    demo_duality()
    demo_characters()
    demo_representative()
    demo_separation()
    print()
    print("All demonstrations completed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

demos.name: Characters, Exponentials and the Rigidity of Divided Powers
demos.description: A focused demonstration of the character theory of both structures. For a chosen plane it verifies that the Kleene star is a character for concatenation but not for the shuffle, that the exponential is a character for the shuffle but not for concatenation, and it tabulates side by side the values exp(l)(a^n), f(a)^n / n! and l*(a^n) to display the divided-power identity that every shuffle character is forced to satisfy. It then checks that the only common point of the two character families is the counit, and that the infinitesimal characters of the concatenation structure — the linear forms obeying the derivation rule g(uv) = g(u)eps(v) + eps(u)g(v) — are exactly the planes, by testing a plane, a degree-two form and a degree-zero form.

demos.name: Shuffle Stability of Rationality and the Factorial Hankel Obstruction
demos.description: Computes exact Hankel ranks for several rational series (the letter-counting series and geometric series) and for their shuffle products, showing that the ranks remain bounded and respect the product bound: the shuffle of the two letter-counting series, each of rank two, has rank exactly four. It then confirms that the shuffle product of series extends the shuffle product of words, by shuffling two indicator series and recovering the multiplicities of the corresponding word shuffle. Finally it isolates the obstruction: the Hankel ranks of the exponential series grow by one at every depth, and every leading minor of the factorial Hankel matrix [1/(i+j)!] is a nonzero rational number, printed exactly.

algorithms.name: Memoized Enumeration of the Shuffle Product with Multiplicities
algorithms.description: The shuffle product of two words is the multiset of all their interleavings, defined by the recursion 1 sh v = v, u sh 1 = u, and au sh bv = a(u sh bv) + b(au sh v). Because the shuffle is a multiset, interleavings arising from different position sets are counted separately, and the total multiplicity is the binomial coefficient C(|u|+|v|, |u|) — the multiplicity of a repeated word can therefore exceed one, which is the combinatorial source of all the factorials appearing later in the theory. A naive implementation costs Theta(C(m+n,m)(m+n)) since the output itself has that many terms; memoizing on the pair of suffix indices reduces the number of distinct recursive calls to (m+1)(n+1), so the coefficient vector is produced in time proportional to the number of *distinct* resulting words times (m+1)(n+1). This routine is the primitive on which every other computation in the pipeline is built: coproduct checks, character tests and Hankel matrices all reduce to shuffle enumerations.

algorithms.name: Exact Hankel Rank Certification of Rationality
algorithms.description: By the Kleene–Schützenberger theorem, a function f on words is representative — equivalently its graph is a rational noncommutative series, equivalently it is computed by a finite weighted automaton — exactly when the infinite Hankel matrix H[u][v] = f(uv) has finite rank, and that rank is the minimal dimension of a linear representation f(w) = lambda mu(w) gamma. This algorithm forms the truncated Hankel matrix indexed by all words of length at most d and computes its rank by exact Gaussian elimination over the rationals. With an alphabet of q letters the matrix has (q^{d+1}-1)/(q-1) rows and columns, so the elimination costs O(size^3) field operations; the arithmetic is exact, which matters because the interesting case — the factorial matrix [1/(m+n)!] — has determinants of order 10^-33 by size seven and would be reported as singular by any floating-point routine. A rank sequence that stabilises is a certificate of rationality; a strictly increasing tail is a certificate of non-rationality at the observed depths.
algorithms.code:
"""Exact Hankel rank certification of rationality."""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import product
from math import factorial
from typing import Callable, List, Tuple

Word = Tuple[str, ...]
Series = Callable[[Word], Fraction]


def words_upto(alphabet: str, depth: int) -> List[Word]:
    """All words of length at most `depth`, in shortlex order."""
    out: List[Word] = []
    for n in range(depth + 1):
        out.extend(product(tuple(alphabet), repeat=n))
    return out


def row_reduce(matrix: List[List[Fraction]]) -> Tuple[List[List[Fraction]], List[int]]:
    """Reduced row echelon form over the rationals; returns (rref, pivot columns)."""
    m = [row[:] for row in matrix]
    rows, cols = len(m), (len(m[0]) if m else 0)
    pivots: List[int] = []
    r = 0
    for c in range(cols):
        piv = next((i for i in range(r, rows) if m[i][c] != 0), None)
        if piv is None:
            continue
        m[r], m[piv] = m[piv], m[r]
        p = m[r][c]
        m[r] = [x / p for x in m[r]]
        for i in range(rows):
            if i != r and m[i][c] != 0:
                f = m[i][c]
                m[i] = [x - f * y for x, y in zip(m[i], m[r])]
        pivots.append(c)
        r += 1
        if r == rows:
            break
    return m, pivots


def hankel_matrix(f: Series, alphabet: str, depth: int) -> List[List[Fraction]]:
    """The truncated Hankel matrix H[u][v] = f(uv), rows and columns indexed by
    all words of length at most `depth`."""
    ws = words_upto(alphabet, depth)
    return [[f(u + v) for v in ws] for u in ws]


def hankel_rank(f: Series, alphabet: str, depth: int) -> int:
    """Exact rank of the truncated Hankel matrix."""
    return len(row_reduce(hankel_matrix(f, alphabet, depth))[1])


def certify_rationality(f: Series, alphabet: str, max_depth: int = 5
                        ) -> Tuple[bool, List[int]]:
    """Compute the Hankel ranks up to `max_depth`.

    Returns (stabilised, ranks).  A function is representative - equivalently its
    graph is a rational noncommutative series, equivalently it is computed by a
    finite weighted automaton - exactly when these ranks are bounded, and the
    bound is then the minimal dimension of a linear representation.  A strictly
    increasing tail is a certificate of non-rationality at the observed depths.
    """
    ranks = [hankel_rank(f, alphabet, d) for d in range(1, max_depth + 1)]
    stabilised = len(ranks) >= 2 and ranks[-1] == ranks[-2]
    return stabilised, ranks


if __name__ == "__main__":
    count_a: Series = lambda w: Fraction(sum(1 for a in w if a == "a"))
    geometric: Series = lambda w: Fraction(5) ** len(w)
    exponential: Series = lambda w: Fraction(1, factorial(len(w)))

    print("number of a's :", certify_rationality(count_a, "ab", 3))
    print("5^|w|         :", certify_rationality(geometric, "ab", 3))
    print("1/|w|!        :", certify_rationality(exponential, "a", 6))

algorithms.name: Myhill–Nerode Synthesis of a Minimal Linear Representation
algorithms.description: The hard direction of the Kleene–Schützenberger theorem is constructive, and this is the construction. The rows of the Hankel matrix are the left translates u^{-1}f : s -> f(us), restricted to suffixes of bounded length. If their span is finite dimensional, a greedy scan in shortlex order extracts a maximal independent family, which is a basis of the translate space; the space is stable under each shift operator g -> a^{-1}g, so expressing the shifted basis rows back in the basis produces the matrix mu(a) of that shift. The coordinate vector of f itself is lambda, and evaluating each basis translate at the empty word gives gamma, whence f(w) = lambda mu(w) gamma. The dimension obtained is minimal, being the exact rank of the Hankel matrix. Cost: O(P) row extractions of width S followed by eliminations, i.e. O(P n^2 S) field operations for a representation of dimension n, where P and S count the prefixes and suffixes used. Applied to the series counting the letter a, it returns a two-dimensional representation, confirming the minimal rank of two.
algorithms.code:
"""Myhill-Nerode synthesis of a minimal linear representation."""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import product
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Tuple

Word = Tuple[str, ...]
Series = Callable[[Word], Fraction]
Matrix = List[List[Fraction]]


def words_upto(alphabet: str, depth: int) -> List[Word]:
    out: List[Word] = []
    for n in range(depth + 1):
        out.extend(product(tuple(alphabet), repeat=n))
    return out


def row_reduce(matrix: Matrix) -> Tuple[Matrix, List[int]]:
    m = [row[:] for row in matrix]
    rows, cols = len(m), (len(m[0]) if m else 0)
    pivots: List[int] = []
    r = 0
    for c in range(cols):
        piv = next((i for i in range(r, rows) if m[i][c] != 0), None)
        if piv is None:
            continue
        m[r], m[piv] = m[piv], m[r]
        p = m[r][c]
        m[r] = [x / p for x in m[r]]
        for i in range(rows):
            if i != r and m[i][c] != 0:
                f = m[i][c]
                m[i] = [x - f * y for x, y in zip(m[i], m[r])]
        pivots.append(c)
        r += 1
        if r == rows:
            break
    return m, pivots


def coordinates_in_basis(basis: Matrix, target: List[Fraction]) -> List[Fraction]:
    """Write `target` in terms of the independent rows of `basis`.

    Solved by reducing the augmented system [basis | I] and tracking the
    combinations used to clear each pivot of `target`."""
    n, width = len(basis), len(basis[0])
    augmented = [basis[i][:] + [Fraction(int(i == j)) for j in range(n)]
                 for i in range(n)]
    reduced, pivots = row_reduce(augmented)
    coefficients = [Fraction(0)] * n
    residue = target[:]
    for r, c in enumerate(pivots):
        if c >= width:
            break
        weight = residue[c]
        if weight == 0:
            continue
        for i in range(n):
            coefficients[i] += weight * reduced[r][width + i]
        residue = [x - weight * y for x, y in zip(residue, reduced[r][:width])]
    return coefficients


def minimal_linear_representation(f: Series, alphabet: str, depth: int
                                  ) -> Tuple[List[Fraction], Dict[str, Matrix], List[Fraction]]:
    """Construct (lambda, mu, gamma) with f(w) = lambda mu(w) gamma.

    The construction is Myhill-Nerode / Hankel: the rows of the Hankel matrix are
    the left translates u^{-1}f restricted to suffixes of bounded length; a
    greedy scan extracts a maximal independent family of them, which is a basis
    of the translate space.  Expressing the shifted rows (ua)^{-1}f in that basis
    yields the matrix mu(a) of the shift operator; lambda holds the coordinates
    of f itself, and gamma evaluates each basis translate at the empty word.

    Cost: O(P) row extractions of width S, each followed by an elimination, where
    P and S are the numbers of prefixes and suffixes used; overall
    O(P * n^2 * S) field operations for a representation of dimension n.
    """
    prefixes = words_upto(alphabet, depth)
    suffixes = words_upto(alphabet, depth)

    def row(u: Word) -> List[Fraction]:
        return [f(u + s) for s in suffixes]

    basis_words: List[Word] = []
    basis_rows: Matrix = []
    for u in prefixes:
        candidate = basis_rows + [row(u)]
        if len(row_reduce(candidate)[1]) > len(basis_rows):
            basis_rows = candidate
            basis_words.append(u)
    n = len(basis_words)

    mu: Dict[str, Matrix] = {}
    for a in alphabet:
        matrix: Matrix = [[Fraction(0)] * n for _ in range(n)]
        for i, bw in enumerate(basis_words):
            matrix[i] = coordinates_in_basis(basis_rows, row(bw + (a,)))
        mu[a] = matrix

    lam = coordinates_in_basis(basis_rows, row(()))
    gam = [f(bw) for bw in basis_words]
    return lam, mu, gam


def evaluate(lam: List[Fraction], mu: Dict[str, Matrix], gam: List[Fraction],
             word: Word) -> Fraction:
    """Evaluate the representation: lambda mu(w) gamma."""
    vector = lam[:]
    for a in word:
        vector = [sum((vector[i] * mu[a][i][j] for i in range(len(vector))), Fraction(0))
                  for j in range(len(vector))]
    return sum((v * g for v, g in zip(vector, gam)), Fraction(0))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    count_a: Series = lambda w: Fraction(sum(1 for a in w if a == "a"))
    lam, mu, gam = minimal_linear_representation(count_a, "ab", 2)
    print("dimension:", len(lam))
    print("lambda   :", lam)
    for a, m in mu.items():
        print(f"mu({a})    :", m)
    print("gamma    :", gam)
    for w in [(), ("a",), ("a", "b"), ("b", "a", "b", "a"), ("a", "a", "a")]:
        print(f"  f({''.join(w) or '1':>5}) = {evaluate(lam, mu, gam, w)}"
              f"  (expected {count_a(w)})")

algorithms.name: Duality-Transport Verification of the Deconcatenation Bialgebra Axiom
algorithms.description: The compatibility of the deconcatenation coproduct with the shuffle product — cutting a riffle of two decks in one place equals cutting each deck and riffling the two left halves and the two right halves separately — is the hard axiom of the theory, because its two sides recurse on incompatible data. This routine evaluates both sides independently as multisets of tensors and compares them, and also checks the duality identity that makes the theoretical proof work: the multiplicity of a word z in u shuffle v equals the multiplicity of the pair (u,v) in the unshuffle coproduct of z. Complexity is dominated by the right-hand side, which enumerates the (|u|+1)(|v|+1) pairs of cuts and, for each, a product of two shuffles, so the cost is roughly |u||v| C(|u|+|v|,|u|) multiset insertions; memoizing the shuffle keeps the constant small. On all pairs of words of length at most three over a two-letter alphabet — 225 pairs — the two sides agree exactly.

visualizations.name: The Rationality Divide: Hankel Rank Growth and the Factorial Minors
visualizations.description: Two panels. The left panel plots the exact rank of the truncated Hankel matrix [f(uv)] as a function of the depth, for three rational series — a geometric Kleene star, a quadratic counting series and the letter-counting series, whose ranks flatten immediately — and for the exponential series 1/|w|!, whose rank increases by one at every depth. The right panel explains why: it displays, on a base-ten logarithmic scale with the sign annotated, the determinants of the leading blocks of the factorial Hankel matrix [1/(i+j)!]. They shrink astronomically fast — by size eight the magnitude is below 10^-40 — yet none is zero, so the matrix has infinite rank and the exponential series can never be produced by a finite weighted automaton.
visualizations.code:
"""Visualization: the rationality divide, seen through Hankel ranks.

Left panel  : the rank of the Hankel matrix [f(uv)] as a function of the depth,
              for three rational series (flat lines) and for the exponential of
              a plane (a strictly increasing line).
Right panel : the leading minors of the factorial Hankel matrix [1/(i+j)!] on a
              logarithmic scale - tiny, alternating in sign, but never zero,
              which is exactly why the exponential has infinite rank.

Run with:  python viz_rationality_divide.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import product
from math import factorial, log10
from typing import Callable, List, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Word = Tuple[str, ...]
Series = Callable[[Word], Fraction]


def words_upto(alphabet: str, depth: int) -> List[Word]:
    out: List[Word] = []
    for n in range(depth + 1):
        out.extend(product(tuple(alphabet), repeat=n))
    return out


def rank(matrix: List[List[Fraction]]) -> int:
    m = [row[:] for row in matrix]
    rows, cols = len(m), (len(m[0]) if m else 0)
    r = 0
    for c in range(cols):
        piv = next((i for i in range(r, rows) if m[i][c] != 0), None)
        if piv is None:
            continue
        m[r], m[piv] = m[piv], m[r]
        p = m[r][c]
        m[r] = [x / p for x in m[r]]
        for i in range(rows):
            if i != r and m[i][c] != 0:
                f = m[i][c]
                m[i] = [x - f * y for x, y in zip(m[i], m[r])]
        r += 1
        if r == rows:
            break
    return r


def hankel_rank(f: Series, alphabet: str, depth: int) -> int:
    ws = words_upto(alphabet, depth)
    return rank([[f(u + v) for v in ws] for u in ws])


def determinant(matrix: List[List[Fraction]]) -> Fraction:
    m = [row[:] for row in matrix]
    n, det = len(m), Fraction(1)
    for c in range(n):
        piv = next((i for i in range(c, n) if m[i][c] != 0), None)
        if piv is None:
            return Fraction(0)
        if piv != c:
            m[c], m[piv] = m[piv], m[c]
            det = -det
        det *= m[c][c]
        inv = m[c][c]
        m[c] = [x / inv for x in m[c]]
        for i in range(c + 1, n):
            if m[i][c] != 0:
                f = m[i][c]
                m[i] = [x - f * y for x, y in zip(m[i], m[c])]
    return det


def main() -> None:
    depths = list(range(1, 7))
    kleene: Series = lambda w: Fraction(2) ** len(w)
    count_a: Series = lambda w: Fraction(sum(1 for a in w if a == "a"))
    poly: Series = lambda w: Fraction(len(w)) ** 2
    expo: Series = lambda w: Fraction(1, factorial(len(w)))

    curves = [
        ("Kleene star  2^|w|", kleene, "#38bdf8"),
        ("counting  |w| squared", poly, "#a78bfa"),
        ("counting  number of a's", count_a, "#4ade80"),
        ("exponential  1/|w|!", expo, "#fb7185"),
    ]

    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.8))

    for label, f, colour in curves:
        ranks = [hankel_rank(f, "a", d) for d in depths]
        ax1.plot(depths, ranks, "o-", color=colour, label=label, linewidth=2)
    ax1.set_xlabel("depth $d$ of the Hankel matrix")
    ax1.set_ylabel(r"rank of $[\,f(uv)\,]_{|u|,|v|\leq d}$")
    ax1.set_title("Rational series have bounded Hankel rank;\nthe exponential does not")
    ax1.grid(alpha=.25)
    ax1.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9)

    sizes = list(range(1, 9))
    logs, signs = [], []
    for n in sizes:
        M = [[Fraction(1, factorial(i + j)) for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]
        d = determinant(M)
        logs.append(log10(abs(float(d.numerator) / float(d.denominator))) if d != 0 else 0.0)
        signs.append("+" if d > 0 else "-")
    bars = ax2.bar(sizes, logs, color=["#38bdf8" if s == "+" else "#fb7185" for s in signs])
    for x, y, s in zip(sizes, logs, signs):
        ax2.text(x, y - 3, s, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=11, color="#334155")
    ax2.set_xlabel("size $n$")
    ax2.set_ylabel(r"$\log_{10}\,|\det\,[1/(i+j)!]_{0\leq i,j<n}|$")
    ax2.set_title("Every leading minor of the factorial Hankel\nmatrix is nonzero (sign shown below the bar)")
    ax2.grid(alpha=.25, axis="y")
    ax2.bar_label(bars, labels=[f"{v:.0f}" for v in logs], padding=2, fontsize=8)

    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("rationality_divide.png", dpi=160)
    print("written: rationality_divide.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

visualizations.name: The Multiplicity Landscape of the Shuffle Product
visualizations.description: Two panels showing where the factorials come from. The left panel is the multiplicity spectrum of a single shuffle product: for a chosen pair of words it draws one bar per distinct resulting word, with height equal to its multiplicity. The bars always sum to the binomial coefficient C(|u|+|v|,|u|), while the number of bars is strictly smaller whenever the two words share letters — that collapse is the precise mechanism forcing divided powers on shuffle characters. The right panel shows the extreme case across a whole family: the multiplicity of a^(m+n) in a^m shuffled with a^n is exactly C(m+n,m), drawn as a Pascal heat map on a logarithmic colour scale with the exact integers overlaid.
visualizations.code:
"""Visualization: the multiplicity landscape of the shuffle product.

Left panel  : the multiset u shuffle v for a chosen pair of words, drawn as a bar
              chart of multiplicities.  The bars sum to the binomial coefficient
              C(|u|+|v|, |u|), while the number of distinct bars is smaller
              whenever u and v share letters - that gap is exactly the
              phenomenon which forces divided powers on shuffle characters.
Right panel : the same effect across a whole family: the multiplicity of the
              word a^(m+n) in a^m shuffle a^n is C(m+n, m), displayed as a
              Pascal heat map.

Run with:  python viz_shuffle_multiplicity.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from collections import Counter
from math import comb
from typing import Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

Word = Tuple[str, ...]


def shuffle(u: Word, v: Word) -> Counter:
    """The multiset of interleavings of u and v, with multiplicity."""
    if not u:
        return Counter({v: 1})
    if not v:
        return Counter({u: 1})
    out: Counter = Counter()
    for z, m in shuffle(u[1:], v).items():
        out[(u[0],) + z] += m
    for z, m in shuffle(u, v[1:]).items():
        out[(v[0],) + z] += m
    return out


def main() -> None:
    u, v = tuple("aab"), tuple("ab")
    spectrum = shuffle(u, v)
    labels = ["".join(z) for z in sorted(spectrum)]
    values = [spectrum[z] for z in sorted(spectrum)]

    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12.5, 4.8))

    ax1.bar(range(len(values)), values, color="#7dd3fc", edgecolor="#0ea5e9")
    ax1.set_xticks(range(len(values)))
    ax1.set_xticklabels(labels, rotation=90, fontsize=7, family="monospace")
    ax1.set_ylabel("multiplicity in $u \\sqcup\\!\\sqcup v$")
    ax1.set_title(f"$u = {''.join(u)}$, $v = {''.join(v)}$:  "
                  f"{len(values)} distinct words, total multiplicity {sum(values)} "
                  f"$= \\binom{{{len(u)+len(v)}}}{{{len(u)}}} = {comb(len(u)+len(v), len(u))}$")
    ax1.grid(alpha=.2, axis="y")

    N = 9
    grid = np.zeros((N, N))
    for m in range(N):
        for n in range(N):
            grid[m, n] = comb(m + n, m)
    im = ax2.imshow(np.log10(grid), origin="lower", cmap="magma")
    ax2.set_xlabel("$n$")
    ax2.set_ylabel("$m$")
    ax2.set_title("multiplicity of $a^{m+n}$ in $a^m \\sqcup\\!\\sqcup a^n$,\n"
                  "equal to $\\binom{m+n}{m}$ (log scale)")
    for m in range(N):
        for n in range(N):
            ax2.text(n, m, str(int(grid[m, n])), ha="center", va="center",
                     fontsize=6, color="white" if grid[m, n] > 100 else "black")
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax2, label="$\\log_{10}$ multiplicity")

    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("shuffle_multiplicity.png", dpi=160)
    print("written: shuffle_multiplicity.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

interactive_demos.title: The Shuffle Laboratory: Products, Coproducts, Duality and the Two Axioms
interactive_demos.description: A four-panel workbench for the combinatorics of the free monoid. Panel one computes the shuffle product of any two words you type, displaying each result with its multiplicity and checking the total against the binomial coefficient — type a and a to meet the factor of two that drives the whole theory. Panel two shows both coproducts of a word side by side: the unshuffle coproduct with its 2^|w| position splittings, and the deconcatenation coproduct with its |w|+1 cuts. Panel three tabulates, term by term, the duality theorem asserting that the multiplicity of a word z in u shuffled with v equals the multiplicity of the pair (u,v) in the unshuffle coproduct of z — the two sides are computed from independent definitions. Panel four verifies both bialgebra axioms live, first on the pair you typed and then, at the press of a button, over all 225 pairs of words of length at most three.
interactive_demos.html:
The Shuffle Laboratory

Two words can be multiplied in two different ways, and each multiplication has a partner that takes words apart. Type any two words over the letters a, b, c and watch the shuffle product, the unshuffle coproduct and the deconcatenation coproduct appear — then check, live, the duality and the two bialgebra axioms that tie them together.

1 · The shuffle product u ш v

The shuffle is a multiset: interleavings coming from different position sets are counted separately, even when the resulting words coincide. Try a and a: the answer is 2·aa, not aa. That factor of two is the seed of the factorials that appear later.

2 · The two coproducts of a word

Unshuffle Δш(w) — split the positions of w into two complementary sets (2|w| terms):
Deconcatenation Δconc(w) — cut w at one of its |w|+1 cut points:

3 · Duality

The two structures are transposes of each other: the multiplicity of a word z in u ш v equals the multiplicity of the pair (u,v) in Δш(z). Every row below is one instance of that theorem, computed from the two definitions independently.

4 · The two bialgebra axioms

A product and a coproduct are compatible when taking apart a product is the same as multiplying the pieces. Both structures satisfy their axiom — the second one (cutting a riffle = riffling the halves) is the hard theorem, proved by transporting the whole computation through the duality above.

interactive_layout:
# Two Ways to Multiply a Word *A guided tour of the shuffle product, the two bialgebras it lives in, and the moment where combinatorics and analysis part company.* --- ## 1. Start with a riffle Take two words, say $ab$ and $c$. Think of each as a small stack of cards, and riffle them together, keeping the internal order of each stack. There are exactly three results: $$ab \sqcup\!\sqcup c \;=\; abc + acb + cab.$$ That operation — write it $\sqcup\!\sqcup$ — is the **shuffle product**. It is associative and, unlike concatenation, *commutative*. Everything on this page grows from one small observation about it: > The shuffle is a **multiset**. Shuffling $a$ with $a$ gives $aa$ **twice**, not once, > because the two cards came from different stacks. In general the total number of interleavings is $$|u \sqcup\!\sqcup v| \;=\; \binom{|u|+|v|}{|u|},$$ the number of ways to choose which positions of the merged word came from $u$. Play with it before reading on. Type any two words below and watch the multiset appear; try $u = a$, $v = a$, then $u = ab$, $v = ab$, and see how many distinct words you get compared with the binomial count. {{interactive_demo:0}}
Click to reveal the formal definition and the proof of the binomial count The shuffle is defined by the recursion $$1 \sqcup\!\sqcup v = \{v\},\qquad u \sqcup\!\sqcup 1 = \{u\},\qquad (au) \sqcup\!\sqcup (bv) = a\cdot\bigl(u \sqcup\!\sqcup bv\bigr) + b\cdot\bigl(au \sqcup\!\sqcup v\bigr),$$ where $a\cdot S$ prefixes the letter $a$ to every element of the multiset $S$. The recursion terminates because $|u|+|v|$ strictly decreases. *Cardinality.* Write $m = |u|$, $n = |v|$. By induction the two branches contribute $\binom{m-1+n}{m-1}$ and $\binom{m+n-1}{m}$ interleavings, and Pascal's rule assembles them into $\binom{m+n}{m}$. $\blacksquare$ *Commutativity* is a double induction on $|u|,|v|$: the recursion is symmetric once the two summands are exchanged. *Associativity* is a strong induction on $|u|+|v|+|w|$, matching the three ways of choosing which of the three leading letters is emitted first. Related reading: [shuffle algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuffle_algebra), [free monoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_monoid).
--- ## 2. Every product needs a partner A product fuses two things; a **coproduct** takes one thing apart in all possible ways at once. Words admit two natural ways of being taken apart. **By position** — choose a subset $S$ of the positions of $w$, read the letters at $S$ as one word and the rest as another: $$\Delta_{\sqcup\!\sqcup}(w) \;=\; \sum_{S} w|_S \otimes w|_{S^{c}} \qquad (2^{|w|}\text{ terms}).$$ This is the **unshuffle coproduct**; equivalently it is the unique rule compatible with concatenation that makes every single letter *primitive*, $\Delta_{\sqcup\!\sqcup}(a) = a\otimes 1 + 1\otimes a$. **By cutting** — slice $w$ at one of its $|w|+1$ cut points: $$\Delta_{\mathrm{conc}}(w) \;=\; \sum_{w = z_1 z_2} z_1\otimes z_2.$$ This is the **deconcatenation coproduct**. Pair them correctly and you get two bialgebras on the same space of noncommutative polynomials $K\langle X\rangle$: | structure | product | coproduct | flavour | |---|---|---|---| | first | concatenation | unshuffle | noncommutative, cocommutative | | second | shuffle | deconcatenation | commutative, co-noncommutative | Panel 2 of the widget above shows both coproducts of any word you type. Panel 3 shows the theorem that ties the two tables together. > **Duality Theorem.** The multiplicity of a word $w$ in $u \sqcup\!\sqcup v$ equals the > multiplicity of the pair $(u,v)$ in $\Delta_{\sqcup\!\sqcup}(w)$. Both numbers count the same objects: the ways to two-colour the positions of $w$ so that the first colour spells $u$ and the second spells $v$.
Click to reveal: the two bialgebra axioms, and why one is much harder A product and a coproduct are *compatible* when taking apart a product equals multiplying the pieces. On the concatenation side this is a one-line induction: $$\Delta_{\sqcup\!\sqcup}(uv) = \Delta_{\sqcup\!\sqcup}(u)\,\Delta_{\sqcup\!\sqcup}(v),$$ because a two-colouring of the positions of $uv$ is just a two-colouring of those of $u$ together with one of those of $v$. On the shuffle side the corresponding statement is $$\Delta_{\mathrm{conc}}(u \sqcup\!\sqcup v) \;=\; \Delta_{\mathrm{conc}}(u)\ \sqcup\!\sqcup_2\ \Delta_{\mathrm{conc}}(v), \qquad (p_1\otimes p_2)\sqcup\!\sqcup_2(q_1\otimes q_2) = (p_1\sqcup\!\sqcup q_1)\otimes(p_2\sqcup\!\sqcup q_2),$$ in words: *cutting a riffle of two decks in one place is the same as cutting each deck and riffling the two left halves and the two right halves separately.* This one has no convenient recursion, because the two sides recurse on incompatible data. The trick is not to prove it directly. Compute the coefficient of a fixed tensor $z_1 \otimes z_2$ on each side; use the Duality Theorem to convert every shuffle count into an unshuffle count; and both sides become the *same* fourfold sum $$\sum_{p}\sum_{q}\sum_{r}\sum_{s} [p_1 = r_1][q_1 = r_2][p_2 = s_1][q_2 = s_2],$$ differing only in the order in which the four summations are performed. Transposing a quadruple sum is a triviality, and the theorem falls out. Choosing the right side of the mirror makes the work evaporate.
The algorithm below is the computational shadow of that proof: it evaluates both sides independently and compares them as multisets. {{algorithm:3}} --- ## 3. Who are the multiplicative functions? For a bialgebra, the interesting objects are its **characters**: scalar-valued functions turning the product into ordinary multiplication of numbers, with value $1$ on the unit. Characters are the "points" of an algebra. For concatenation the answer is complete and clean. Call a family of scalars $(c_x)_{x\in X}$ a **plane** $\ell = \sum_x c_x x$, and let its **Kleene star** be $\ell^{*} = 1 + \ell + \ell^{2} + \cdots$, whose coefficient at $x_1\cdots x_n$ is $c_{x_1}\cdots c_{x_n}$. > **Theorem (concatenation characters).** $f$ satisfies $f(1)=1$ and $f(uv)=f(u)f(v)$ if and > only if $f = \ell^{*}$ for a unique plane $\ell$, namely $c_x = f(x)$. > > **Theorem (infinitesimal characters).** $g$ satisfies the derivation rule > $g(uv) = g(u)\varepsilon(v) + \varepsilon(u)g(v)$, where $\varepsilon(w)=1$ for the empty > word and $0$ otherwise, if and only if $g$ vanishes on every word of length $\neq 1$ — > that is, if and only if $g$ is a plane. For the shuffle the characters look completely different: > **Theorem (shuffle characters).** For any plane $\ell$, the series with coefficient > $c_{x_1}\cdots c_{x_n}/n!$ at $x_1\cdots x_n$ — the exponential $\exp(\ell)$ — is a > character of the shuffle algebra. Moreover *every* shuffle character $f$ obeys the > divided-power identity $f(a^{n}) = f(a)^{n}/n!$. The factorials are forced, not chosen. Run the demonstration to see all four statements checked on explicit numbers. {{demo:1}}
Click to reveal the proofs (they are short) *Why $\exp(\ell)$ is a shuffle character.* Shuffling permutes letters without creating or destroying them, so every $z \in u \sqcup\!\sqcup v$ has the same letter-weight $C_uC_v$ and the same length $m+n$. Hence $$\sum_{z \in u \sqcup\!\sqcup v} \exp(\ell)(z) \;=\; \binom{m+n}{m}\frac{C_uC_v}{(m+n)!} \;=\; \frac{C_u}{m!}\cdot\frac{C_v}{n!},$$ using $\binom{m+n}{m}m!\,n! = (m+n)!$. It is the identity behind $e^{x}e^{y} = e^{x+y}$, transported to words. *Why divided powers are forced.* Shuffling $n$ identical cards with one more gives the same word $n+1$ times: $a^{n} \sqcup\!\sqcup a = (n+1)\,a^{n+1}$. So any shuffle character has $f(a^{n})f(a) = (n+1)f(a^{n+1})$, and induction gives $f(a^{n}) = f(a)^{n}/n!$. That single multiplicity — the $2$ in $a \sqcup\!\sqcup a = 2\,aa$ — is the seed of every factorial that follows. *Why the two families barely overlap.* If a Kleene star $\ell^{*}$ were a shuffle character, the same identity at $n=1$ would give $c_x^{2} = 2c_x^{2}$, so $c_x = 0$ for every letter. The only common point is the counit.
--- ## 4. What a finite machine can compute A third notion now enters: **rationality**. Call $f$ **representative** when the two-variable function $(u,v)\mapsto f(uv)$ factors through a finite sum, $$f(uv) \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{n} g_i(u)\,h_i(v).$$ Intuitively: to know $f$ on $uv$, you need only finitely many numbers about $u$. That intuition is a theorem. > **Kleene–Schützenberger Theorem.** For $f : X^{*}\to K$ with $K$ a field, the following are > equivalent: > 1. $f$ is representative; > 2. the left translates $w^{-1}f : u \mapsto f(wu)$ span a finite dimensional space; > 3. there are vectors $\lambda,\gamma$ and matrices $\mu(x)$, one per letter, with > $f(w) = \lambda\,\mu(w)\,\gamma$ where $\mu$ is extended multiplicatively. Condition (2) is the practical test: form the **Hankel matrix** $H = [\,f(uv)\,]$ with rows indexed by $u$ and columns by $v$, and measure its rank. Bounded rank means rational; growing rank means not. {{algorithm:1}} And the passage from a finite-rank Hankel matrix to actual matrices $\mu(x)$ — the Myhill–Nerode construction, the heart of the theorem's hard direction — is itself an algorithm you can run: {{algorithm:2}}
Click to reveal: the cycle of implications **(1) ⟹ (2)** The factorization exhibits every translate inside the span of $h_1,\dots,h_n$, since $w^{-1}f = \sum_i g_i(w)\,h_i$. **(2) ⟹ (3)** Let $V$ be the span of the translates, of dimension $n$. It contains $f$ itself and is stable under each shift $g \mapsto a^{-1}g$, because the shift of a generator is a generator. Let $\mu(a)$ be the matrix of the shift in a basis of $V$; let $\lambda$ be the coordinate vector of $f$; let $\gamma_i$ be the value of the $i$-th basis vector at the empty word. Then $\lambda\mu(w)\gamma = (w^{-1}f)(1) = f(w)$. **(3) ⟹ (1)** Expand $\mu(uv) = \mu(u)\mu(v)$ and read off the finite sum over matrix entries. Related reading: [rational series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rational_series), [weighted automata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weighted_automaton).
Rational functions are also closed under everything algebraic in sight — sums, scalars, pointwise products, and (less obviously) the shuffle product of series $$(f \sqcup\!\sqcup g)(w) \;=\; \sum_{(u,v)\in \Delta_{\sqcup\!\sqcup}(w)} f(u)\,g(v),$$ whose stability follows directly from the bialgebra axiom $\Delta_{\sqcup\!\sqcup}(uv) = \Delta_{\sqcup\!\sqcup}(u)\Delta_{\sqcup\!\sqcup}(v)$, with rank bounded by the product of the two ranks. {{demo:2}} --- ## 5. The chasm Now put the two character families against the rationality test. This is the punchline of the whole story, and you can discover it yourself in the laboratory below: select the Kleene star family and watch the ranks stay flat, then select the exponential family and watch them climb by one at every depth. {{interactive_demo:1}} > **Separation Theorem.** Over the real numbers, let $\ell$ be a plane with $c_a \neq 0$ for > some letter $a$. Then $\exp(\ell)$ is a character of the shuffle algebra but is **not** a > representative function, while $\ell^{*}$ is a representative function of rank one but is a > character of the shuffle algebra only in the degenerate case $\ell = 0$. The two character > groups meet exactly in the counit. Why? Along the powers of a single letter, the Hankel matrix of $\exp(\ell)$ is the factorial matrix $[\,1/(m+n)!\,]$, and that matrix has infinite rank.
Click to reveal the Archimedean squeeze that kills the factorial matrix Suppose $\sum_{i\le N} g_i/(n+i)! = 0$ for every $n \ge 0$. Fix the smallest index $k$ whose coefficient is not yet known to vanish and multiply the relation by $(n+k)!$. The $k$-th term becomes exactly $g_k$; every later term picks up a factor $$\frac{(n+k)!}{(n+i)!} \;\le\; \frac{1}{n+k+1}\qquad (i > k),$$ because the denominator has at least one extra factor of size $\ge n+k+1$. Hence $|g_k| \le M/(n+k+1)$ with $M = \sum_i |g_i|$ a fixed constant — for *every* $n$. Letting $n$ grow gives $g_k = 0$. Nothing deeper than "factorials outrun any constant". $\blacksquare$ Equivalently, the leading minors of $[1/(i+j)!]$ are $$1,\ -\tfrac12,\ -\tfrac1{144},\ \tfrac1{1036800},\ \tfrac1{1463132160000},\ \dots$$ — vanishingly small, alternating in sign, never zero.
The two pictures below make the divide visible: on one side, ranks that flatten; on the other, ranks that climb forever, with determinants that shrink towards zero without ever reaching it. {{visualization:0}} And the picture that explains *where the factorials came from* in the first place — the multiplicity landscape of the shuffle: {{visualization:1}} --- ## 6. What it means Step back. The space of noncommutative polynomials carries two bialgebra structures that are formal mirror images. Each has a perfectly describable set of characters. On the concatenation side the characters are exactly the objects finite automata love: Kleene stars, rank-one rational series. On the shuffle side the characters are exponentials, carrying divided powers and factorial denominators — exactly the objects no finite automaton can produce. The dictionary between the two sides is perfect at the level of the algebra: shuffle and unshuffle are transposes, both compatibility axioms hold, rationality survives the shuffle product. It is only at the level of *points* that the worlds refuse to overlap. There is a concrete moral. The shuffle algebra is the algebra of iterated integrals: the [signature of a path](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rough_path) multiplies by the shuffle rule and is group-like for the unshuffle coproduct. The Separation Theorem says that a nondegenerate signature is never a rational series — its factorial decay, the very property that makes truncated signatures such effective features in data analysis, is precisely the obstruction to finite-state computability. The most satisfying part is how much is carried by a single multiplicity. That $a \sqcup\!\sqcup a = 2\,aa$ rather than $aa$ seeds the divided powers; the divided powers seed the factorials; the factorials seed the Hankel obstruction; and the Hankel obstruction is the chasm. One factor of two, patiently followed, separates two universes. --- ## 7. Run everything The complete tour — shuffle basics, duality, both bialgebra axioms, characters, divided powers, Kleene–Schützenberger, shuffle stability of rationality and the separation theorem — in one self-contained script with exact rational arithmetic: {{demo:0}} And the shuffle enumerator that underlies all of it: {{algorithm:0}}
